lead: Electric power steering (EPS) replaces the hydraulic pump, belt and fluid with an electric motor that pushes the steering only when the driver asks. A torque sensor measures how hard the driver turns; a speed signal says how fast the car is going; the ECU (electronic control unit) looks up an assist map and sets motor current. Parking needs a large assist, highway driving a small one. EPS is common on new cars in India, from hatchbacks to SUVs, and it provides the steering actuator for lane-keeping in ADAS.
prereq: You need: torque and angle sensors and the Hall effect (automotive sensors and actuators), and the 12 V supply and motor currents (vehicle electrical systems).

sections.h3: From hydraulic to electric: where the motor sits

blocks.text: Conventional hydraulic power steering drives its pump from the engine belt; electro-hydraulic systems keep the hydraulic rack but drive the pump with an electric motor. The pump circulates oil even when the wheel is straight, so it costs fuel. A rotary valve sends pressure to one side of the rack when the driver turns. EPS removes the pump, the belt and the fluid. An electric motor provides torque only when the driver moves the wheel, so straight-line running draws almost no steering power.

There are three common layouts. In column EPS the motor sits on the steering column and drives it through a worm gear; this is compact and suits small cars. In pinion EPS the motor turns a second pinion on the rack, while the driver turns the first pinion; this is the dual-pinion layout. In rack EPS the motor turns a ball screw that pushes the rack directly, giving the largest assist for heavier cars.
The motor does not drive the rack directly. A reduction gear multiplies its torque. If the gear ratio is N, the assist torque at the pinion is:

T<sub>assist</sub> is assist torque at the pinion in N·m (gear losses ignored); N is the reduction ratio, unitless; k<sub>t</sub> is the motor torque constant in N·m per ampere; I<sub>m</sub> is motor current in A.

The driver's torque and the assist add at the pinion: T<sub>pinion</sub> = T<sub>driver</sub> + T<sub>assist</sub>. T<sub>driver</sub> is the torque the driver applies through the steering wheel, in N·m.

The torque sensor is the heart of EPS. It uses a torsion bar: a thin shaft between the steering wheel input and the pinion output. When the driver turns, the bar twists by a small angle. The twist angle is proportional to driver torque. A Hall-effect or inductive pick-up measures the relative angle between the two ends, without touching them. Zero twist means zero driver torque, so the ECU can set zero assist.

A separate steering angle sensor measures how far the steering wheel is turned from straight ahead, over several turns lock to lock; dividing by the steering ratio gives the road-wheel angle. It uses geared magnets and Hall sensors, or an optical code disc. The angle signal is needed for return-to-centre, for damping, and by ESP. The speed signal arrives over the CAN bus from the ABS unit.

The sensor pair must be plausible. A torque sensor signal outside its range, or a signal that does not match the angle sensor, sets a fault code. The ECU then reduces assist or shuts the motor down, because a wrong torque reading could give a large assist in the wrong direction.

sections.h3: The assist map, damping and adaptive ratio

blocks.text: The assist map is a look-up table. One axis is driver torque, the other is vehicle speed. The output is target assist torque, or directly a target motor current. At parking speed the map allows a large assist, perhaps 40 N·m at the pinion, so a small driver torque moves the tyres on dry tarmac. At 120 km/h the map allows only a small assist, perhaps 4 N·m, so the driver still feels the road. More assist is not better at speed; it makes the wheel numb and hides the limit of grip.

Three corrections sit on top of the map. Return-to-centre adds a small torque that brings the wheel back after a low-speed turn, so the driver does not have to unwind it by hand. Damping opposes fast steering motion; it is computed from the rate of change of angle and prevents overshoot when the driver releases the wheel. Friction compensation adds a small current to overcome the column, gear and rack friction, so the steering feels light and consistent.

Fail-safe is mechanical. If the motor, sensor or ECU fails, a relay or clutch disconnects the motor. The column and rack still connect the wheel to the road, so the driver steers manually with higher effort. The ECU also limits motor current and temperature; a stalled motor at full lock must not burn.

Adaptive or variable-ratio steering goes further. An active steering system fits a planetary gear and a second motor in the column. At low speed it adds angle, so a small turn of the wheel gives a large road-wheel angle; at high speed it subtracts angle, so the car is less twitchy. The same ECU changes both ratio and assist with speed. Some syllabi call the whole area adaptive power steering.

spec.aria: Steering wheel, torsion bar, column and pinion in a column; a motor with a 16 to 1 worm drives the column; the ECU reads torque and speed and sets current; a table gives 40 and 4 newton metres of assist, 2.5 and 0.25 newton metres of motor torque, 50 and 5 amperes.

examples.question: A car with column EPS is parked. Turning the tyres needs 44 N·m at the pinion; the driver gives 4 N·m and the assist map asks for the other 40 N·m. At 120 km/h the map asks for only 4 N·m of assist. The worm reduction is 16 : 1, the motor torque constant is 0.05 N·m per ampere and the pinion radius is 8 mm. Ignore gear losses. Find (a) the rack force at parking and (b) the motor torque and motor current at both conditions.
steps: Pinion torque at parking: T<sub>pinion</sub> = T<sub>driver</sub> + T<sub>assist</sub> = 4 + 40 = 44 N·m.
Rack force = pinion torque ÷ pinion radius = 44 N·m ÷ 0.008 m = 5500 N, or 5.5 kN.
The worm multiplies motor torque by 16 on its way to the pinion, so the motor needs T<sub>assist</sub> ÷ N = 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5 N·m.
Motor current at parking: I<sub>m</sub> = 2.5 N·m ÷ 0.05 N·m/A = 50 A.
Motor current at 120 km/h: I<sub>m</sub> = 0.25 ÷ 0.05 = 5 A.

Check with the formula: N × k<sub>t</sub> × I<sub>m</sub> = 16 × 0.05 × 50 = 40 N·m and 16 × 0.05 × 5 = 4 N·m. The 50 A parking peak sets the size of the EPS fuse and cable; at speed the current, and the assist, are a tenth of that.
examples.answer: Rack force 5.5 kN at parking; motor torque 2.5 N·m and current 50 A at parking, 0.25 N·m and 5 A at 120 km/h.

traps: More assist is not always better: assist must fall as vehicle speed rises, otherwise the steering feels numb and the driver loses road feel.
Steering torque is the driver's input measured by the torsion bar; assist torque is the motor's output at the pinion. They are not the same quantity.

Going from the motor to the pinion, multiply by N; going back from the assist the map asks for to the motor torque, divide by N, as the worked example does. Using the wrong direction makes the current 256 times wrong for a 16 : 1 gear.
The torque sensor measures twist across the torsion bar; the steering angle sensor measures absolute wheel position. Swapping their roles breaks return-to-centre and ESP.
Fail-safe does not mean the motor keeps assisting. It means the motor is disconnected and the driver still has a mechanical path to the road wheels.

quiz.q: What does an EPS system use instead of hydraulic pressure to assist the driver?
quiz.a: An electric motor, a reduction gear and a controlled motor current; the ECU sets the current from the assist map.

quiz.q: Why does the assist map reduce assist torque as vehicle speed increases?
quiz.a: At high speed the tyres need less steering torque and the driver needs road feel. Too much assist makes the wheel numb and can hide the limit of grip, so the map limits assist at speed.

quiz.q: An assist map asks for 30 N·m at the pinion. The reduction ratio is 15 : 1 and the motor constant is 0.04 N·m/A. Find the motor torque and motor current.
quiz.a: Motor torque = 30 ÷ 15 = 2 N·m. Motor current = 2 ÷ 0.04 = 50 A.

quiz.q: A car has very heavy steering at parking speed but normal steering at 80 km/h. The motor and reduction gear are healthy. Which signal or map is the likely cause, and why?
quiz.a: Check the vehicle speed signal and the low-speed part of the assist map first. Heavy steering only at parking points to the map not giving large assist at low speed, or a speed signal that wrongly reports a high speed. A torque sensor fault would usually affect both conditions.

quiz.q: What is the job of the torsion bar in the torque sensor?
quiz.a: It twists by an angle proportional to driver torque, and a Hall or inductive pick-up measures that twist angle.

quiz.q: What happens in the steering system when EPS fails electrically?
quiz.a: A relay or clutch disconnects the motor. The column and rack still connect the wheel to the road, so the driver steers manually with higher effort.

quiz.q: Why is a dual-pinion layout used instead of driving the rack from the same pinion that the driver turns?
quiz.a: It separates the driver's mechanical path from the motor's assist path. The motor can apply assist through its own pinion without adding backlash or friction to the driver's pinion, and the packaging suits larger cars.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production EPS is moving to 48 V and integrated motor controllers, which reduce current and wiring size. Steer-by-wire removes the mechanical column but keeps a redundant motor and fault-tolerant ECU, so fail-safe becomes fail-operational. Calibration of the assist map is a major tuning task; it uses measured steering torque, yaw rate and driver preference.
